activity.text: spent two days at the Gartner Marketing Symposium/Xpo in London, and it was one of the most energizing events I’ve attended in a long time — not because of the technology (although the AI sessions were outstanding), but because of the conversations about what it means to lead today. Dylan Alcott AO opened with a keynote on authenticity, vulnerability and perspective. Born with a tumor wrapped around his spinal cord, he spent his early years in and out of hospitals before becoming one of the most decorated athletes in history: Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball and tennis, 15‑time Grand Slam champion, and the first person with a disability to be named Australian of the Year. What stayed with me was not the medals, but how he spoke about owning his story. He reminded us that vulnerability creates connection — and that perspective is a daily choice. In a corporate world that often rewards armor, his message was a powerful reminder that humanity is a strategic advantage. Tali Sharot, Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at UCL PALS, shifted the lens to the science of influence. Her research shows that people don’t change because we warn them — they change when we offer hope, agency and a sense of progress. A timely insight as we navigate AI adoption and new operating models. Alexandra Earl session on “Who Are the Successful Change Leaders of Today?” brought the data: – Only 32% of leaders achieve healthy change adoption – Employees trust change less than ever – The most effective leaders don’t inspire harder — they routinize change, build emotional safety, and coach teams to develop “change reflexes” that make adaptation intuitive. Across the AI sessions, one theme kept emerging: AI is not the strategy — it’s an enabler. In pharma, this matters even more. AI can help us understand patient journeys faster, identify unmet needs earlier, and design more precise, more inclusive engagement models. It can augment how we shape markets, how we support HCPs, and how we bring clarity to complex decisions. But at its core, AI is simply a means to an end: helping more patients access the treatments they need, when they need them. The real impact comes when we combine AI’s analytical power with human judgment, empathy and purpose. Technology can accelerate insights — but it’s leaders who turn those insights into better access, better experiences and better outcomes. My reflection: The future belongs to leaders who can combine the best of AI with the best of being human — empathy, curiosity, courage, and the ability to move others toward possibility. Today I’ve been reflecting on the neuro‑dynamics of power — not the kind written in org charts, but the kind we feel. What we call “power dynamics” often mirrors our inner world: our fears, our conditioning, the stories we carry from our past and even from those before us. We think we’re reacting to reality, but most of the time we’re reacting to our own wiring. And when inner safety is missing, we cling to control, to certainty, to being busy. We fear change, we fear AI, we fear losing relevance — sometimes we even fear being ourselves. The best leaders I’ve met share something simple: They trust their teams. They invite ideas and challenge. They create safety without announcing it. They take responsibility and give credit away. They make people feel seen. Today I want to honour those leaders — the ones who choose courage over control and humanity over ego. If someone like that has inspired you, tell them. Leadership can be lonely, and your words might matter more than you think. #Leadership #HumanLeadership #SelfAwareness #Neuroscience ...more

I don’t know about you, but Eileen Gu’s recent comments about neuroplasticity, self-awareness and consciously shaping who she wants to become have stayed with me since the Olympics. Her message wasn’t just about sport - it was about ownership. It was a reminder that the best athletes don’t leave performance to chance. They train their minds as intentionally as their bodies. In my view, leadership is no different. As women, we are often encouraged to be resilient, adaptable, strong. But resilience is not something we are born with - it’s built. Confidence is not a personality trait - it’s practiced. Leadership is not a title - it’s a decision - to challenge our limiting beliefs, invest in our development and take radical responsibility for our actions, behaviors, decisions and growth. On this International Women’s Day, I'm reflecting on the importance of taking ownership of who we choose to be. In the meantime, I'll keep working on my skiing!! #IWD2026 #ForAllWomenAndGirls #Leadership #WomenInLeadership #OwnYourGrowth tagging few women who continue inspiring me... 🤖 “Relax, the robots aren’t taking our job…” That’s what I told a colleague after our latest marketing meeting and during few peer conversation @ Impatient Health Pharmageddon and Gartner workshop in paris— right after someone muttered: “With AI, do we even need marketers anymore?” Let’s be real — this question is echoing across every pharma company right now. But here’s the twist 👇 💡 The danger isn’t that AI will replace marketing. The real danger is that marketing ignores AI. 📊 The numbers don’t lie: --> The AI-in-Pharma market will hit $4.35 B by 2025 and $25.7 B by 2030 (42% annual growth). --> AI could unlock $868 B in value across healthcare by 2030. --> But only 15% of pharma orgs are ready to implement AI at scale. --> There are already 13 GenAI use cases in pharma marketing — and counting. We’re investing billions in AI tech… but if we don’t upskill our marketers, that Ferrari will sit idle in the garage. AI can already: 🚀 Turn data into insight. 🧠 Predict customer needs. 💬 Personalise engagement at scale. But without human creativity + strategic thinking, it’s just code. So the question isn’t Marketing or AI — It’s Marketing supercharged with AI. The future belongs to AI-supercharged marketers, not replaced ones. Before the next budget cycle, let's ask ourselves: 👉 Are we funding technology or capability? or should we do both??? 👉 Are we afraid of AI — or training to lead it? Our edge isn’t being human or digital — It’s being human in a digital world. What do you think — threat or ally? Mice don't menstruate. They're also the main animal model in women's health research. Women weren't even required in clinical trials until 1993. And we wonder why AI keeps stalling on the female body. That's where last night's Women Healing Women: AI x Health panel landed for me. Hosted by Women in AI for #HumanTechWeek with Jenny D. (Clair Health), Dr. Christy Lane (FLORA Fertility), and Izzy Nova (micro1), moderated by Bidisa Mukherjee . What I'm still sitting with: ➡️ Infertility is the 3rd highest cost women face ➡️ 1 in 6 couples need fertility treatment. Only 2% can afford it. ➡️ Hormones are still modeled as homeostatic, like glucose. They're not. They're dynamic. ➡️ PCOS is being renamed to PMOS (Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome) to match the biology Jenny showed how non-invasive wearables can finally feed ML models continuous hormone, sleep, stress, and ECG data — treating the female body as the dynamic system it actually is. The unlock for the next 5 years? Every panelist landed in the same place: data democratization. Pool disparate datasets. Share across companies. More women in the room. More institutional backing. Shoutout to Sarah Farrow , whose post last week made the mouse fact stick. The technology isn't the bottleneck. The data foundation is. 🧬

A few months ago, I started training an AI agent called Sophie to help the THRIVE team conduct interviews and gather participant insights for our AI+ Advantage programme. Something I learnt very quickly in this process was that Sophie is incredibly capable at a lot of things, but one of them is not “just getting what I mean.” Apparently vague instructions, half-baked thoughts and “you know… sort of like last time” are not valid briefing techniques for AI agents. As someone who naturally enjoys the big picture rather than the detail, this was both fascinating and deeply irritating. After several rounds of Sophie enthusiastically misunderstanding me and just doing her own thing despite my objections, a generous colleague, Gasser H. , introduced me to Markdown. Suddenly, things started to click. Not because Markdown is magical, it’s actually very simple – that’s the point, but because it forced me to think more clearly, structure instructions properly and communicate with AI-level precision. Turns out the training happening here wasn’t just for the AI. It was also for me. Reading the recent debate about HTML vs Markdown for AI agents on X made me smile because underneath all the technical discussion is a much bigger shift. The skill is no longer just producing the work yourself. It’s knowing how to create the conditions for an agent to work for you. That requires patience, experimentation, curiosity and occasionally a sense of humour when your AI interviewer cuts someone off mid-answer and enthusiastically moves onto the next question. Agentic AI can still feel intimidating and strangely alien. But honestly, most of us do not need to become engineers to start using these tools well. We just need the willingness to learn some new skills. And yes… I suppose the overused line is true: AI probably won’t take your job. But someone who knows how to work with AI might.
